drills.q: Define the test pyramid and the testing trophy, and state what each optimizes for.
drills.a: Pyramid (Cohn, 2009): many unit, some integration, few E2E -- optimizes for speed/cost. Trophy (Dodds, 2018): static analysis, heavy integration, some unit, thin E2E -- optimizes for confidence per test written.

drills.q: Name three categories of code you should explicitly never write a test for, and why each wastes effort.
drills.a: Third-party library internals (that's the library's own test suite's job); trivial delegation methods (the test just re-asserts the implementation); framework wiring already proven by one smoke test (per-instance tests add no new information).

drills.q: A team has 90% unit coverage and monthly production incidents traced to integration bugs. What's the actual fix, and why won't more unit tests help?
drills.a: The suite is pyramid-shaped in an architecture where behavior lives at component boundaries; heavy mocking structurally hides bugs like wrong SQL joins or serialization mismatches. Fix is adding an integration layer with real dependencies (e.g., via Testcontainers) at those boundaries -- more unit tests with the same mocking style reproduce the same blind spot.

drills.q: A refactor that changes internal structure but not behavior breaks 40 tests. Diagnose and state the fix.
drills.a: The tests assert on implementation details (mock call sequences, private method calls) instead of observable behavior through the public interface. Fix: rewrite to assert on outputs and side effects visible to a caller, which also removes the ongoing maintenance tax on future refactors.

drills.q: When is a pyramid-shaped test suite still the correct choice in 2026, and what changes if that codebase later grows external dependencies?
drills.a: Correct for libraries, SDKs, or algorithm-heavy code where the function signature is the actual product surface and units are genuinely isolated pure logic. If the codebase grows real external dependencies (a cache, a DB), the shape should shift toward more integration-layer tests -- clinging to the original pyramid shape as the system evolves is the actual common failure.

drills.q: Explain why static analysis sits at the base of the testing trophy and is described as 'free,' and name what it definitely does not catch.
drills.a: It runs on every save/commit, catching type mismatches, unreachable code, and null-safety violations before any test executes, at near-zero marginal cost per line once tooling exists. It does not catch logic errors or wrong business rules -- code that is type-correct but semantically wrong (e.g., double-charging tax) requires actual tests.

drills.q: Justify cutting an 80-spec E2E suite down to 15 specs to a skeptical staff engineer, using real reasoning rather than a slogan.
drills.a: Identify the 15 as the genuinely revenue-critical, cross-system journeys (login, checkout, core workflow); show the remaining 65 either duplicate integration-test coverage or cover low-impact paths relative to their flakiness and CI runtime cost. Back the argument with measured flake rate and CI time, not a general 'keep E2E thin' principle.

drills.q: What is the relationship between test strategy (pyramid/trophy) and mutation testing, and why doesn't a high mutation score replace the strategy decision?
drills.a: Test strategy decides which layer (unit/integration/E2E) deserves investment for a given architecture; mutation testing measures whether the tests actually written in that layer verify behavior or merely execute code. They are orthogonal -- a codebase can have the right layer allocation with weak tests in that layer, or the wrong layer allocation with strong tests in the wrong place.

drills.q: A junior engineer proposes deleting a flaky E2E test that caught a real regression a month ago. How do you reason about this tradeoff as a senior engineer?
drills.a: Name the tradeoff explicitly rather than picking a side by default: an occasional missed edge case caught late is often cheaper in aggregate than a permanently slow, low-trust CI pipeline engineers route around -- but if that specific journey is high-risk (revenue, compliance), the cost of missing it can outweigh the flakiness tax, and that risk assessment, not a blanket rule, decides it.

drills.q: State the full five-step decision procedure for whether and how to test a given piece of behavior.
drills.a: 1) Can static analysis already catch this class of bug (route there, not to a test). 2) Is it complex pure logic -- unit test, consider property-based testing. 3) Does it only manifest with a real collaborator (DB/cache/queue) -- integration test with real deps via Testcontainers. 4) Is it a top revenue-critical journey spanning the whole system -- thin E2E. 5) Is it a cross-team/cross-repo API boundary -- contract test (Pact), not integration test.
